findings.claim: Study the code and its output carefully, because this exact pattern — combining a string, an integer and a real number in one line — appears constantly in exam tasks.
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about exam frequency. Neither the 1CP2 specification extract nor the PLS v6 states anything about how often a particular formatting pattern is set in Paper 2 tasks; the PLS simply gives this as an illustrative example.
findings.correction: Study the code and its output carefully, because this example from the PLS combines all three options — a string, an integer and a real number — in one format string.

findings.claim: The number of placeholders in the string does not match the number of values given to .format(), which raises an error.
findings.problem: Only wrong in one direction. Verified in Python 3: "{:d} {:d}".format(1) raises IndexError, but supplying more values than placeholders is silently ignored — "{}".format(1, 2, 3) returns '1' with no error. As written the claim is factually incorrect for surplus values.
findings.correction: Giving .format() fewer values than there are placeholders raises an error (an IndexError); note that surplus values are simply ignored, so a mismatch will not always be reported.

findings.claim: {"q": "What error occurs if the number of placeholders doesn't match the number of values in .format()?", "a": "Python raises an IndexError."}
findings.problem: The card is factually wrong as stated: an IndexError is raised only when there are too few values. Verified in Python 3 that extra values are ignored without error, so a 'mismatch' does not always produce an error.
findings.correction: {"q": "What error occurs if .format() is given fewer values than there are placeholders?", "a": "Python raises an IndexError; surplus values, by contrast, are ignored silently."}

findings.claim: round (<x>, <n>) changes the actual value stored, so later maths uses the rounded figure.
findings.problem: Imprecise. The PLS v6 built-in subprograms table describes round as returning a rounded value ('Rounds <x> to the number of <n> digits after the decimal'); it does not modify the variable passed to it. round(total, 2) leaves total unchanged unless the result is assigned.
findings.correction: round (<x>, <n>) returns a new rounded number, so if you store that result, later maths uses the rounded figure.

findings.claim: {"q": "What is the key difference between round(x, 2) and a format placeholder like {:.2f}?", "a": "round() changes the stored value; the placeholder only changes the display."}
findings.problem: Same imprecision as the body text: round() returns a rounded value rather than altering the variable given to it (PLS v6, built-in subprograms table).
findings.correction: {"q": "What is the key difference between round(x, 2) and a format placeholder like {:.2f}?", "a": "round() returns a rounded value you can store and reuse; the placeholder only changes how the value is displayed."}

findings.claim: only use the exact subprogram names and argument order shown in the PLS — markers can only credit constructs listed there ... anything else risks losing marks even if it draws correctly in your own editor.
findings.problem: Contradicts the PLS v6 Introduction (the source text), which states that Pearson will not go beyond the PLS when setting tasks but that a student successfully using constructs not included in the document will still be awarded marks in Paper 2 if the solution is valid. The assertion about what markers can credit and about 'losing marks' is an unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour.
findings.correction: Stick to the subprogram names and argument order shown in the PLS: everything Pearson sets can be solved with PLS constructs, and the PLS is supplied as an insert so you can check them in the exam. (The PLS does note that a valid solution using constructs outside the subset will still be awarded marks, but working inside the subset is the safest, quickest route.) If a trace table question involves random.randint, remember it can return either endpoint you specify, so work out both extremes when reasoning about possible values.

findings.claim: constant — A named value provided by a library module that never changes, such as math.pi for the value of pi.
findings.problem: Wrong definition of a constant. The PLS states only that 'Constants are conventionally named in all uppercase characters', and specification point 6.3.2 treats constants as ordinary program values; a constant is any named value that does not change while the program runs, not something that must come from a library module. As written, a student defining 'constant' in a 2-mark Define question would give a non-creditable answer.
findings.correction: constant — A named value that is set once and does not change while the program runs; constants are conventionally named in all uppercase characters. Library modules can also supply constants, such as math.pi for the value of pi.

findings.claim: parameter — A value passed into a subprogram when it is called, which the subprogram uses while it runs.
findings.problem: This is the definition of an argument, not a parameter, and it duplicates the lesson's own (correct) 'arguments' entry, so the two glossary terms contradict each other. A parameter is the named variable in the subprogram definition (e.g. <paramA> in def <procname> (<paramA>, <paramB>): in the PLS Subprograms table) that receives the argument value when the subprogram is called.
findings.correction: parameter — A variable named in a subprogram's definition, such as <paramA> in def calculate (paramA, paramB):, which receives the value of the matching argument when the subprogram is called.

findings.claim: time.sleep (<sec>) pauses the program for the number of seconds given as its parameter.
findings.problem: Terminology inconsistent with the lesson's own (correct) definition of 'arguments' earlier in the same lesson: the value supplied in the call, e.g. the 1 in time.sleep(1), is an argument; <sec> is the parameter in the PLS definition.
findings.correction: time.sleep (<sec>) pauses the program for the number of seconds given as its argument.

findings.claim: Filling: call <turtle>.begin_fill () before drawing a shape, set <turtle>.fillcolor (<colour>), then call <turtle>.end_fill () once the shape is complete.
findings.problem: The stated order contradicts the lesson's own worked example, which correctly sets t.fillcolor("blue") before t.begin_fill(). The PLS describes fillcolor as setting the colour used to fill and begin_fill as being called 'just before drawing a shape to be filled', so the fill colour should be set first to avoid confusion.
findings.correction: Filling: set <turtle>.fillcolor (<colour>), call <turtle>.begin_fill () just before drawing the shape, then call <turtle>.end_fill () once the shape is complete.

findings.claim: Leaving out turtle.done () at the end of a drawing program, so the window closes immediately instead of staying open.
findings.problem: Overstated: the PLS says the turtle window closes as soon as the program completes only 'in some development environments', and it gives two ways to keep it open — turtle.done () or a final input () line.
findings.correction: Leaving out turtle.done () at the end of a drawing program, so that in some development environments the window closes as soon as the program finishes (a final input () line also keeps it open, though scrollbars will not work).

findings.problem: Stray space between the object name and the dot; the PLS writes this as <turtle>.left (<degrees>), and turtle .left(degrees) as printed is not the form students should copy.
